screens.title: Incident Detection, Analysis, and Containment
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll walk through the high-stakes steps that follow preparation: detecting an incident, analyzing what happened, and containing the threat while keeping evidence intact. You'll learn where alerts commonly come from, how analysts triage and scope a compromise, and the containment actions that limit damage without destroying crucial forensic data. Detection failures increase dwell time — attackers stay longer and can do more harm — while rushed containment can erase the very artifacts you need to prove root cause. We'll use practical examples, including a point-of-sale server contacting a known malicious host, to compare containment trade-offs like host isolation versus careful segmentation. You will also practice questions an analyst asks during triage and the single most important evidence types to preserve before taking disruptive action. By the end you will be able to decide containment approaches that balance evidence preservation, business continuity, and safety, and you will be prepared to document every step. Consider what you already do when an alert appears — this chapter will sharpen the questions you ask and the order in which you act.

screens.title: What is Detection?
screens.narratorSegment: Detection is simply the act of discovering that a security event or compromise exists. In practice detection comes from multiple sources with differing visibility and fidelity: SIEM correlates logs from many systems to flag suspicious sequences, IDS/IPS inspects network traffic for signatures or anomalies, EDR watches endpoint behavior for suspicious processes or file changes, antivirus detects known malware, threat intelligence provides indicators of compromise you can match, and user reports supply human-observed anomalies. Each source has strengths and weaknesses. SIEM excels at spotting multi-system patterns but depends on good log coverage and tuning. EDR gives deep endpoint context but only where an agent is present. User reports often detect social engineering that automated tools miss. A common misconception is to treat every alert as equally reliable; instead, learn to weigh alert source and contextual evidence. For example, a SIEM alert that shows repeated failed logins followed by a successful access from an odd IP plus matching EDR process execution is stronger than a single antivirus detection with no other signs. Good detection practice blends telemetry, human reports, and threat intelligence so you can prioritize real incidents and reduce false positives. What detection signals do you already rely on, and how would you validate their reliability?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Detection is identifying that an incident occurred using telemetry, tools, and human reports.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › What is Detection?
Definition
Recognizing a security event through telemetry and reports
Detection sources differ in coverage and confidence. Combine signals to strengthen your conclusions and reduce false positives.
SIEM: correlates multi-system logs to spot patterns.
EDR: shows process activity, file changes, and endpoint context.
IDS/IPS: inspects network traffic for signatures or anomalies.
User reports & threat feeds: human and external intelligence.
Concrete example
A SIEM flags multiple failed logins, then a successful login from an unusual IP and an outbound connection to a known command-and-control host. EDR shows a suspicious child process and file changes. Together these signals indicate a higher-confidence incident than any single alert alone.
Common misconception: Treating all alerts equally. Not all alerts carry the same weight; context matters.
Why this matters: Early, accurate detection reduces dwell time and limits adversary impact across systems.
Key Takeaway: Combine telemetry and reports to prioritize real incidents.

screens.title: SIEM Alerts — Interpreting Correlated Signals
screens.narratorSegment: SIEM systems turn large volumes of logs into prioritized alerts by correlating events with detection rules. When you receive a SIEM alert, don't treat it as the final answer — use it as a starting point. Begin by verifying the event timeline: when did the suspicious activity start, which accounts and hosts are involved, and what other correlated events exist? A useful concrete example is an alert for multiple failed logins followed by a successful login from an unusual IP and an outbound connection to a known malicious host. In that case, confirm the log sources' timestamps, check for EDR process data on the endpoint, and look for network flows showing the outbound connection. Beware of common misconceptions: a SIEM alert alone is not proof of a breach; missing logs or misconfigured timezones can create false context. Also avoid acting without preserving evidence — for example, blocking an IP before capturing live traffic or imaging the endpoint might remove traces you need. Practical steps: assemble the correlated log set, validate sources, cross-check with endpoint and network telemetry, and document your findings. That disciplined approach turns SIEM noise into confident, prioritized response actions.

keyIdea.text: Use SIEM correlations as hypotheses to validate with endpoint and network evidence before acting.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › SIEM Alerts — Interpreting Correlated Signals
Eyebrow: Process
Turn SIEM correlations into validated incidents
Treat SIEM alerts as starting hypotheses. Validate with timestamps, endpoint activity, and network flows before containment actions.
Example alert timeline: 
2024-01-10 09:12: Failed logins (user A)
2024-01-10 09:18: Failed logins (user A)
2024-01-10 09:21: Successful login (user A) from unusual IP
2024-01-10 09:23: Outbound connection to 192.0.2.10
Validation checklist
  • Confirm log timestamps and synchronization across sources.
  • Pull EDR process and file activity for the endpoint in question.
  • Capture or request recent network flow data to verify outbound connections.
  • Check threat intelligence for the external IP or domains mentioned.
Common mistake: blocking an IP before capturing flow data or imaging the host.
Key Takeaway: Validate SIEM hypotheses with endpoint and network evidence.

screens.title: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR)
screens.narratorSegment: EDR agents provide detailed visibility into endpoint activity: process execution, child processes, file modifications, registry changes, and sometimes memory artifacts. This granular view lets analysts see what actually ran on a host, which is crucial for scoping and initial root cause hypotheses. For example, if a SIEM alert points to a suspicious login, EDR can show whether a new process spawned a command shell and wrote files related to a data exfiltration tool. That kind of detail turns a high-level alert into an actionable incident. A common misconception is that EDR alone is sufficient; it is powerful, but only where agents are deployed and functioning. EDR data should be combined with network telemetry and logs to map attacker movement. Practical implications: during triage, check the EDR timeline, export relevant process trees, and collect memory artifacts if needed. Remember evidence preservation: if you plan to isolate or reboot a host, capture volatile EDR data first. Good practice integrates EDR into the triage checklist rather than relying on it as the single source of truth. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) means edr gives granular endpoint context that supports scoping and initial root cause hypotheses.. In practical terms, why endpoint visibility matters for analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › EDR — Why endpoint visibility matters
Definition
EDR records process, file, and memory activity on endpoints
EDR turns filesystem and process activity into evidence you can analyze for scoping and root-cause hypotheses.
Process trees and child processes
File modifications and handles
Memory artifacts and live telemetry
Concrete example
EDR shows that a scheduled task spawned cmd.exe which wrote a DLL to a system folder and opened a remote socket. Combined with SIEM outbound flow logs, this confirms active exfiltration attempts.
Misconception: EDR is a single source of truth. It must be correlated with network and log data.
Pro tip: Export process trees and capture volatile memory before rebooting or isolating the host.
Key Takeaway: Use EDR to turn alerts into concrete endpoint evidence for scoping.

screens.title: IDS/IPS and Network Telemetry
screens.narratorSegment: IDS and IPS systems analyze network traffic to detect signatures or anomalous patterns. An IDS typically alerts you to suspicious flows, while an IPS can actively block or modify traffic. Network telemetry is essential for confirming outbound command-and-control channels, lateral movement, or data exfiltration. For example, if a compromised host makes repeated connections to a known malicious IP, network flow records corroborate endpoint findings. However, signatures alone can be evaded by encryption or novel techniques, so combine network data with endpoint and log evidence. Common mistakes include relying on a single sensor's rule set or failing to collect sufficient packet captures before changing firewall rules. Packet captures and flow logs are often the best sources for proving exfiltration or C2 activity in later analysis or legal proceedings. During triage, request recent network flows and, when necessary, capture live PCAPs for the suspected timeline. Remember that blocking a C2 address may force an adversary to change tactics, so consider preserving traffic records before taking irreversible network actions. IDS/IPS and Network Telemetry means network telemetry verifies communications and shows lateral movement; preserve flows and packet captures before disruptive network changes.. In practical terms, detecting malicious patterns and blocking at the network layer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › IDS/IPS and Network Telemetry
Definition
IDS/IPS and flow logs reveal communications and signs of lateral movement
Network telemetry corroborates and extends endpoint evidence, and is often decisive for proving data flows to external hosts.
Flow logs: show TCP/UDP connections and volumes.
PCAPs: packet-level records useful for detailed analysis and legal evidence.
IPS actions: can block or rate-limit suspicious traffic.
Concrete example
Network flows show repeated small uploads from a server to an external IP over several hours. Combined with EDR file reads, this pattern indicates staged exfiltration rather than a one-off connection.
Misconception: Blocking C2 immediately is always best. Blocking before capturing flows can remove critical evidence.
Pro tip: If you must block quickly, capture recent flows and a PCAP snapshot first.
Key Takeaway: Preserve network evidence before irreversible network containment steps.

screens.title: Analysis Phase — Triage to Root Cause
screens.narratorSegment: Analysis is the central investigative phase. Begin with triage: quickly determine whether the alert is a false positive or a bona fide incident and assign initial severity. Useful triage tasks include checking log integrity, looking for supporting telemetry, and confirming the affected host's operational state. Next, scope the incident by identifying affected systems, accounts, and data. This requires digging into logs, EDR timelines, and network flows to answer how many machines are involved, what data could be impacted, and how long the adversary has been present. After scoping, perform a severity assessment that maps impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability; that formal severity guides resource allocation and stakeholder communication. Finally, perform an initial root cause analysis to hypothesize access vector — phishing, unpatched vulnerability, or credential compromise — so containment targets the cause rather than a symptom. Common pitfalls include stopping at triage without thorough scoping, or treating an initial root cause as final. Evidence preservation is ongoing: document every step, collect forensic images and volatile data where appropriate, and keep chains of custody. The analysis phase is iterative and should produce clear, documented hypotheses you can test with additional data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Analysis Phase — Triage to Root Cause
Process
Structured analysis: triage, scope, severity, root cause
Step 1 — Triage: verify the alert, check timestamps, and confirm the host status.
Step 2 — Scoping: enumerate affected hosts, accounts, and potential data exposures.
Step 3 — Severity: map impact to confidentiality, integrity, availability and business impact.
Step 4 — Initial root cause: form testable hypotheses about how access was achieved.
Supporting cards
Example: a compromised server requires you to check outbound connections, process lists, recent user logins, scheduled tasks, and file changes to determine scope and likely vector.
Common mistake: stopping after triage. Without scoping you may miss lateral movement.
Key Takeaway: Analysis should produce testable, documented hypotheses that guide containment and forensics.

screens.title: Triage — Quick, Accurate Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: Triage is the rapid assessment step that separates false positives from genuine incidents and assigns an initial severity level for response. Effective triage answers a handful of immediate questions: is the alert supported by reliable telemetry, is the affected system critical to operations, are there signs of active malicious behavior, and how many systems might be affected? For example, in a POS server alert with outbound connections to a known skimmer IP, triage should confirm the outbound connection via network flows, verify active processes on the POS server via EDR, and check whether transactions are impacted. Common triage errors include overclassifying low-confidence alerts as high severity, or underclassifying alerts that show rapid lateral movement. Use a consistent checklist: timestamp validation, source credibility, cross-sensor corroboration, and impact estimate. Triage is intentionally quick, but it must produce a clear go/no-go decision for containment and evidence collection. Document your decision and what evidence you used so later analysis and stakeholders understand why initial actions were taken. Triage — Quick, Accurate Assessment means quickly confirm incidents and assign severity using cross-sensor checks and a consistent checklist.. In practical terms, deciding if an event is an incident and assigning preliminary severity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core Concept
Rapidly determine incident validity and priority
Triage yields a fast, evidence-backed decision that directs containment and forensics.
Checklist: validate timestamps, source credibility, corroborate with EDR/network, estimate impact.
Pitfall: mislabeling severity due to incomplete context.
Scenario example
Alert: POS server outbound to known skimmer IP. Triage actions: verify flow logs, pull EDR process tree, check transaction integrity, and identify criticality of the host.
Documentation: record what was checked, initial severity, and the justification for containment actions.
Key Takeaway: A structured checklist speeds triage and reduces misclassification.

screens.title: Scoping the Compromise
screens.narratorSegment: Scoping determines the full extent of a compromise: how many hosts, which accounts, and what data may be affected. This step requires methodical queries across logs, EDR timelines, and network flows. Begin with the initial host and follow indicators of compromise — for example, examine process child relationships, scheduled tasks, account login histories, and outbound connections shown in flow logs. Expand scope iteratively: list directly affected systems first, then search for lateral movement indicators such as unusual authentication events, unknown services running, or beaconing traffic patterns. A practical example is a compromised server that had an account used on other hosts; you must check those hosts for the same artifact or suspicious activity. Common scoping mistakes are stopping early or assuming only the initially observed host is affected. Use automated queries where possible to search programmatically for shared indicators, but validate results manually before containment. Accurate scoping ensures containment efforts cover the true blast radius and prevents re-emergence after remediation. Scoping the Compromise means expand from the initial host to identify all affected systems, accounts, and potential data exposures before final containment.. In practical terms, finding affected systems, accounts, and data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Severity Assessment and the CIA Triad
screens.narratorSegment: Severity assessment maps the incident's technical scope to business impact using confidentiality, integrity, and availability as lenses. Confidentiality concerns whether sensitive data may have been exposed; integrity asks whether data or systems were altered; availability asks if critical services are disrupted. Assigning severity levels — Critical, High, Medium, Low — helps prioritize resources and communications. Severity should guide containment urgency and stakeholder notification. screens.title: Evidence Preservation
screens.narratorSegment: Evidence preservation is the continuous practice of collecting and protecting digital artifacts needed for analysis and possibly legal proceedings. Key items include full forensic disk images, volatile memory dumps, running process lists, open network connections, and relevant logs. The sequence matters: volatile data should be captured before powering down or otherwise altering a system. A frequent and costly mistake is to shut off a server or reboot it immediately, which can erase memory-resident indicators and break the chain of custody for later analysis. For example, before isolating a POS server suspected of exfiltration, capture a memory dump, export EDR timeline data, and request recent network flows or a PCAP snapshot. Securely store collected artifacts with clear documentation of who collected them, when, and how. If you must act quickly to stop ongoing damage, try to collect minimal volatile data first and document the trade-off. Evidence preservation ensures that root cause analysis, legal actions, and post-incident reviews have the required artifacts to be reliable and defensible. Evidence Preservation means capture volatile and persistent artifacts in a documented, secure way before disruptive containment steps when possible.. In practical terms, collecting forensic images, volatile data, and logs safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.7 › Evidence Preservation
Definition
Collect and protect artifacts before they are changed or destroyed
Prioritize volatile data capture: memory dumps, running processes, and open connections. Then collect persistent images and logs.
Volatile: memory dumps, process lists, open network sockets.
Persistent: forensic disk images and log archives.
Documentation: chain of custody, who collected what and when.
Concrete caution
Do not power down a compromised host before capturing volatile memory or process data if you need those artifacts. If immediate action is required to stop active harm, capture what you can and document what you could not.
Common mistake: performing containment that destroys evidence, then trying to reconstruct events from incomplete records.
Key Takeaway: Preserve volatile artifacts before irreversible containment when feasible, and always document trade-offs.

screens.title: Containment Strategies: Short-Term vs Long-Term
screens.narratorSegment: Containment aims to limit spread and impact while preserving evidence and business continuity. Short-term containment stops immediate damage: host isolation disconnects a compromised machine, network segmentation prevents lateral movement, service shutdown disables the exploited service, and account disablement removes compromised credentials. These are fast and direct but can disrupt operations if used indiscriminately. Long-term containment is strategic: re-architecting network segments, deploying stronger detection, or patching vulnerable systems to prevent re-entry. A critical trade-off is speed versus completeness. For example, isolating a POS server may stop a skimmer, but you may lose volatile evidence and interrupt transactions. Conversely, network segmentation can preserve some business functions but may be slower and require coordination. Common mistakes include acting too quickly without scoping, over-containment that unnecessarily halts business processes, and under-containment that leaves attack paths open. Good practice documents the decision, aims for reversible steps when possible, and considers how the adversary may react — blocking a C2 might trigger a destructive payload. Choose containment with both technical and business context in mind. In practical terms, choosing reversible actions that limit spread and preserve operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Short-Term Containment
Network segmentation: isolate subnets or hosts via firewall/VLAN changes.
Host isolation: disconnect a compromised host entirely; effective but disruptive.
Service shutdown & account disablement: stop vectors quickly with less network change.
Long-Term Containment
Actions to prevent re-emergence and strengthen detection.
Re-architecting segments, deploying additional EDR coverage, and improving logging retention.
Pros and cons: long-term steps reduce recurrence but require planning and downtime windows.
Key Takeaway: Combine short-term measures that stop spread with long-term fixes to prevent re-entry.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll walk through the high-stakes steps that follow preparation: detecting an incident, analyzing what happened, and containing the threat while keeping evidence intact. You'll learn where alerts commonly come from, how analysts triage and scope a compromise, and the containment actions that limit damage without destroying crucial forensic data. Detection failures increase dwell time — attackers stay longer and can do more harm — while rushed containment can erase the very artifacts you need to prove root cause. We'll use practical examples, including a point-of-sale server contacting a known malicious host, to compare containment trade-offs like host isolation versus careful segmentation. You will also practice questions an analyst asks during triage and the single most important evidence types to preserve before taking disruptive action. By the end you will be able to decide containment approaches that balance evidence preservation, business continuity, and safety, and you will be prepared to document every step. Consider what you already do when an alert appears — this chapter will sharpen the questions you ask and the order in which you act.

By the end of this chapter you will identify common detection sources, perform rapid triage and scoping, choose containment strategies, and preserve evidence to support later analysis or legal action. First, you'll recognize alerts coming from SIEM, IDS/IPS, EDR, antivirus, user reports, and threat intelligence. Knowing the source helps you prioritize and interpret the signal. Next, you'll use triage techniques to confirm true incidents and assign preliminary severity that drives resource allocation. You'll also practice scoping to determine how many systems and what data were affected. Third, you'll learn containment options — short-term actions like host isolation or service shutdown, and long-term measures such as segmentation — and when each is appropriate. Finally, you'll learn the essential steps for evidence preservation: taking forensic images, capturing volatile memory, and securely storing logs before disruptive actions. Each objective links technical skills to real operational trade-offs and business impact, so you'll be ready to act under pressure while protecting evidence and minimizing unnecessary disruption.

This second objectives slide links skills to real challenges you will face on the job. You'll learn to ask the right triage questions to separate false positives from real incidents, and to scope compromises fully so you don't miss affected systems. We'll practice assessing severity against confidentiality, integrity, and availability to prioritize actions that protect business operations. You'll also study common early-phase mistakes: acting too quickly and destroying evidence, or under-containment that allows lateral movement. Finally, you'll learn to document decisions and make containment actions reversible when possible. Together these competencies help you balance speed and caution under pressure. We'll ground this practice in a realistic point-of-sale compromise where you must weigh immediate shutdown against preserving live forensic data. The goal is to make well-reasoned decisions that consider evidence preservation, business impact, and the adversary's possible reactions.

Detection is simply the act of discovering that a security event or compromise exists. In practice detection comes from multiple sources with differing visibility and fidelity: SIEM correlates logs from many systems to flag suspicious sequences, IDS/IPS inspects network traffic for signatures or anomalies, EDR watches endpoint behavior for suspicious processes or file changes, antivirus detects known malware, threat intelligence provides indicators of compromise you can match, and user reports supply human-observed anomalies. Each source has strengths and weaknesses. SIEM excels at spotting multi-system patterns but depends on good log coverage and tuning. EDR gives deep endpoint context but only where an agent is present. User reports often detect social engineering that automated tools miss. A common misconception is to treat every alert as equally reliable; instead, learn to weigh alert source and contextual evidence. For example, a SIEM alert that shows repeated failed logins followed by a successful access from an odd IP plus matching EDR process execution is stronger than a single antivirus detection with no other signs. Good detection practice blends telemetry, human reports, and threat intelligence so you can prioritize real incidents and reduce false positives. What detection signals do you already rely on, and how would you validate their reliability?

SIEM systems turn large volumes of logs into prioritized alerts by correlating events with detection rules. When you receive a SIEM alert, don't treat it as the final answer — use it as a starting point. Begin by verifying the event timeline: when did the suspicious activity start, which accounts and hosts are involved, and what other correlated events exist? A useful concrete example is an alert for multiple failed logins followed by a successful login from an unusual IP and an outbound connection to a known malicious host. In that case, confirm the log sources' timestamps, check for EDR process data on the endpoint, and look for network flows showing the outbound connection. Beware of common misconceptions: a SIEM alert alone is not proof of a breach; missing logs or misconfigured timezones can create false context. Also avoid acting without preserving evidence — for example, blocking an IP before capturing live traffic or imaging the endpoint might remove traces you need. Practical steps: assemble the correlated log set, validate sources, cross-check with endpoint and network telemetry, and document your findings. That disciplined approach turns SIEM noise into confident, prioritized response actions.

EDR agents provide detailed visibility into endpoint activity: process execution, child processes, file modifications, registry changes, and sometimes memory artifacts. This granular view lets analysts see what actually ran on a host, which is crucial for scoping and initial root cause hypotheses. For example, if a SIEM alert points to a suspicious login, EDR can show whether a new process spawned a command shell and wrote files related to a data exfiltration tool. That kind of detail turns a high-level alert into an actionable incident. A common misconception is that EDR alone is sufficient; it is powerful, but only where agents are deployed and functioning. EDR data should be combined with network telemetry and logs to map attacker movement. Practical implications: during triage, check the EDR timeline, export relevant process trees, and collect memory artifacts if needed. Remember evidence preservation: if you plan to isolate or reboot a host, capture volatile EDR data first. Good practice integrates EDR into the triage checklist rather than relying on it as the single source of truth. Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) means edr gives granular endpoint context that supports scoping and initial root cause hypotheses.. In practical terms, why endpoint visibility matters for analysis. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IDS and IPS systems analyze network traffic to detect signatures or anomalous patterns. An IDS typically alerts you to suspicious flows, while an IPS can actively block or modify traffic. Network telemetry is essential for confirming outbound command-and-control channels, lateral movement, or data exfiltration. For example, if a compromised host makes repeated connections to a known malicious IP, network flow records corroborate endpoint findings. However, signatures alone can be evaded by encryption or novel techniques, so combine network data with endpoint and log evidence. Common mistakes include relying on a single sensor's rule set or failing to collect sufficient packet captures before changing firewall rules. Packet captures and flow logs are often the best sources for proving exfiltration or C2 activity in later analysis or legal proceedings. During triage, request recent network flows and, when necessary, capture live PCAPs for the suspected timeline. Remember that blocking a C2 address may force an adversary to change tactics, so consider preserving traffic records before taking irreversible network actions. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Analysis is the central investigative phase. Begin with triage: quickly determine whether the alert is a false positive or a bona fide incident and assign initial severity. Useful triage tasks include checking log integrity, looking for supporting telemetry, and confirming the affected host's operational state. Next, scope the incident by identifying affected systems, accounts, and data. This requires digging into logs, EDR timelines, and network flows to answer how many machines are involved, what data could be impacted, and how long the adversary has been present. After scoping, perform a severity assessment that maps impact to confidentiality, integrity, and availability; that formal severity guides resource allocation and stakeholder communication. Finally, perform an initial root cause analysis to hypothesize access vector — phishing, unpatched vulnerability, or credential compromise — so containment targets the cause rather than a symptom. Common pitfalls include stopping at triage without thorough scoping, or treating an initial root cause as final. Evidence preservation is ongoing: document every step, collect forensic images and volatile data where appropriate, and keep chains of custody. The analysis phase is iterative and should produce clear, documented hypotheses you can test with additional data.

Triage is the rapid assessment step that separates false positives from genuine incidents and assigns an initial severity level for response. Effective triage answers a handful of immediate questions: is the alert supported by reliable telemetry, is the affected system critical to operations, are there signs of active malicious behavior, and how many systems might be affected? Containment aims to limit spread and impact while preserving evidence and business continuity. Short-term containment stops immediate damage: host isolation disconnects a compromised machine, network segmentation prevents lateral movement, service shutdown disables the exploited service, and account disablement removes compromised credentials. These are fast and direct but can disrupt operations if used indiscriminately. Long-term containment is strategic: re-architecting network segments, deploying stronger detection, or patching vulnerable systems to prevent re-entry. A critical trade-off is speed versus completeness. For example, isolating a POS server may stop a skimmer, but you may lose volatile evidence and interrupt transactions. Conversely, network segmentation can preserve some business functions but may be slower and require coordination. Common mistakes include acting too quickly without scoping, over-containment that unnecessarily halts business processes, and under-containment that leaves attack paths open. Good practice documents the decision, aims for reversible steps when possible, and considers how the adversary may react — blocking a C2 might trigger a destructive payload. Choose containment with both technical and business context in mind. Keep four central ideas in mind: detection is multi-source and must be validated; analysis is structured and produces testable hypotheses; preservation of volatile and persistent evidence is essential before irreversible actions; and containment should balance immediate risk reduction with business continuity and forensics. Detection sources like SIEM, EDR, IDS/IPS, antivirus, threat feeds, and user reports each add context. Analysis uses triage, scoping, and severity assessment to guide resource allocation. Evidence preservation—memory dumps, forensic images, and captured flows—protects your ability to perform root cause analysis and support legal needs. Containment includes short-term actions like isolation and segmentation and long-term measures like re-architecting networks. The right response is a documented, reversible-minded sequence that minimizes harm while preserving the information you need to learn from the incident. Second, preserve volatile evidence—memory and live connections—before disruptive containment when feasible. Third, choose containment that minimizes re-emergence while maintaining critical business functions and documenting reversible steps.
